title: Three Roads and a Tree's Warning
subtitle: Milk or blood marks the brothers' fortunes

learningObjectives.text: What does milk from a brother's notch mean?
Which direction does the eldest prince choose?

notches.work: Fairy Tales From Far and Near
notches.author: Katherine Pyle
notches.locator: Pyle retelling · The Princes And The Friendly Animals; Pyle retelling · The Princes And The Friendly Animals, normalized characters 2328-3261
notches.excerpt: The three brothers then asked their stepsister which of them she would follow, and she said she would go with the eldest Prince, for she too wished nothing better than a place to dwell in, where she could live in peace and safety. So the three brothers parted, but first the eldest Prince cut three notches in a tree that stood at the parting of the ways. He cut one at the East, and one at the West, and one in the center between them, one for each of his brothers, and one for himself. He told them the notch to the East was for the youngest brother, the notch to the West was for the second brother, and the one in the center belonged to himself. “When any one of us returns to this spot,” said he, “let him place his finger first upon one notch, and then upon the other. If milk flows forth from the notch, then all is well with the one to whom it belongs, but if blood flows forth, then it means death or misfortune to that one.
notches.note: Verbatim text from Katherine Pyle's 1922 English children's retelling. The collection labels it Lithuanian but does not identify an oral informant or underlying source text.

narrativeBlocks.title: The family parts at a crossroads
narrativeBlocks.body: The youngest prince chooses east, the second west, and the eldest chooses the road straight ahead. Their stepsister goes with the eldest.

narrativeBlocks.title: A sign for each brother
narrativeBlocks.body: Quotation from Pyle's English retelling (whitespace normalized): “The three brothers then asked their stepsister which of them she would follow, and she said she would go with the eldest Prince, for she too wished nothing better than a place to dwell in, where she could live in peace and safety. He cut one at the East, and one at the West, and one in the center between them, one for each of his brothers, and one for himself. He told them the notch to the East was for the youngest brother, the notch to the West was for the second brother, and the one in the center belonged to himself. “When any one of us returns to this spot,” said he, “let him place his finger first upon one notch, and then upon the other. If milk flows forth from the notch, then all is well with the one to whom it belongs, but if blood flows forth, then it means death or misfortune to that one.”

narrativeBlocks.title: The tree records their fortunes
narrativeBlocks.body: The eldest prince cuts a notch for each brother and explains the sign: milk means all is well; blood means death or misfortune.

narrativeBlocks.title: A story device, not a ritual claim
narrativeBlocks.body: The notched tree is a plot device in Pyle's Lithuanian-labeled story. Do not present it as evidence of a documented Baltic divination practice.

narrativeBlocks.title: The sign sets up the next event
narrativeBlocks.body: The brothers' separate roads and the tree's signal give the tale a way to reunite their stories later.
